extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, scholars, and students of scientific method (those seeking to reform or improve inquiry)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and diagnostics for improving natural philosophy/scientific inquiry: signs of error, causes of stagnation, and methodological prescriptions (emphasis on experiment, goals, and institutional obstacles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid declaring inquiries impossible (New Academy skepticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat discoveries or operations as beyond the limits of possibility, nor convert defects of one’s own discoveries into a calumny on nature that deters others from investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns against the attitude that certain things are impossible and thus not to be attempted; such scepticism discourages speculation and industry. Practitioners should not allow perceived difficulty or past failure to be taken as proof of impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat dissension among philosophers as a sign of weak methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Wide variance and long-standing dissensions among philosophical schools indicate the path from senses to understanding was not well prepared and that methods or systems are unsound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the same groundwork (nature of things) leads to widely differing errors, this shows systemic methodological failure; persistence of controversies about particulars implies lack of secure demonstration methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept unanimity as confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Unanimity of opinion is often the product of prejudice, authority, or obsequious concurrence rather than free judgment, and may even be a reason for suspicion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True unanimity requires free judgment arriving at the same conclusion after investigation; popular or historical unanimity should not be treated as proof, and is often an unfavorable sign where it suppresses scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize historical and temporal limits on scientific progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress in the sciences has occurred in comparatively few fruitful epochs; long intervals with little genuine advance are common and partly explain slow overall progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awareness of the uneven distribution of productive ages cautions against expecting uniform progress and highlights the importance of creating favorable conditions (time, institutions) for science to flourish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make natural philosophy the root and continuing nourishment of particular sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular sciences flourish only when continually nourished and informed by natural philosophy; separation from its roots leads to shallow, superficial knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplines (astronomy, optics, medicine, music, mechanics, moral and political philosophy) need to be repeatedly referred back to natural philosophy for depth—natural philosophy should both inform and be informed by applied branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage dedicated practitioners of natural philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural philosophy seldom advances when practitioners are divided among many other pursuits; exclusive or devoted attention (by artisans, monks, or dedicated investigators) aids progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The work recommends fostering conditions where individuals can devote themselves primarily to natural philosophy rather than treating it as mere preparation or handmaid to other arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set the proper end of science: useful inventions and augmentation of human life
rubrics_metrics.description: The legitimate goal of the sciences is practical: to endow human life with new inventions and riches, not merely to satisfy contemplative curiosity or personal fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientists and teachers should aim research toward discovery of effects and applications; using the augmentation of arts and useful works as the test of truth will orient investigation productively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a method starting from the senses and regular, well-conducted experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery should begin with the senses and proceed by regulated, digested experiment leading to axioms and further experiments, rather than with tradition, undirected reflection, or logic alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes methods that gather past opinions, then rely on mental reflection or formal logic; instead, investigators should 'set up a light' (a guiding method) and then conduct experiments in a systematic order to deduce axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize experience: regulated and digested experiment, not chance groping
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience must be constructive and ordered—experiments should be combined and directed to reveal principles; random or desultory trials are ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correct order is to establish a guiding light (method), perform a planned course of experiment, deduce axioms, and then design new experiments from those axioms—opposed to mere groping or untargeted trial-and-error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject disdain for particulars and manual/experimental labor
rubrics_metrics.description: The dignity of the mind is not diminished by prolonged engagement with experiments and particulars; such work is necessary and not 'mean' or unworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let vainglory or prejudice repel investigators from close work with particulars; experimental labor, though tedious, is essential to discovery and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not idolize antiquity or authority; prefer time-tested truth and present inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverence for ancient authors and authority retards progress; truth is 'the daughter of time', not of authority, and the present age may surpass predecessors by accumulated experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators should privilege fresh observations and accumulated experiments of the present over blind deference to ancient texts; proliferation of voyages and observations in the present age yields material unavailable to ancients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware false abundance from mechanical refinements
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent richness in mechanical arts and polished devices can mislead into believing sciences are fuller than they are, because many refinements rest on few axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that skilled manufacture or refined arts may reflect patience and manual skill rather than deep theoretical understanding; do not mistake ornament or dexterity for scientific depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of impostors and extravagant promises that discredit legitimate novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Charlatans who promise prodigious effects (e.g., prolonging life, transmutation, divination) damage the reputation of all new proposals, causing legitimate discoveries to be met with suspicion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel claims, especially those coupled with promises of spectacular effects, must be carefully distinguished from imposture; the conduct of impostors has historically blunted enthusiasm for genuine innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid limiting inquiry to trivial refinements or single narrow aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Focusing only on minor improvements or on investigating an object in isolation produces scant progress; grand discoveries require broader, interconnected investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators should not restrict themselves to narrow tasks (e.g., polishing one invention); rather they should seek connections across objects, since the same nature may manifest differently and illuminate hidden properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and resist superstition and imprudent religious opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Blind religious zeal, superstition, and the improper mixing of divinity with philosophy have impeded natural philosophy by condemning inquiry as impious or by subsuming science under received doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the specific ways religion can block inquiry (accusations of impiety, conflation of sacred mysteries with natural ones, or fear that discoveries will undermine faith) and argue that natural philosophy complements understanding of the divine power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform institutional practices (schools, universities) that repress new thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Current habits and regulations of academies and universities often oppose scientific progress by chaining pursuits to writings of particular authors and punishing dissent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should allow and reward departures from the 'common track' and encourage collaborative advantage rather than enforcing rigid adherence to canonical texts and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align rewards and recognition to support genuine scientific advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Science advancement and social rewards frequently belong to different individuals; lack of proper reward for innovators and poor popular praise inhibit scientific labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creating incentives and recognition structures (beyond mere praise of princes or popular acclaim) is necessary so that innovators are encouraged and supported to undertake demanding investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combat despair and cultivate reasonable hope for success
rubrics_metrics.description: A prevailing belief in impossibility and the prudence that augurs the worst dampen enterprise; preparing minds with hope is essential to encourage experiments and new attempts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author urges providing reasons for optimism (analogous to Columbus’ reasons for new lands) and framing scientific pursuit as plausible and divinely sanctioned, so as to motivate sustained effort rather than resignation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use theological and providential arguments to justify and encourage science (rhetorical support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeal to God and providence as a basis for hope: divine providence leads to gradual increase of knowledge, and the pursuit of natural philosophy is consistent with religious truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When facing religious opposition or popular despair, align the aims of science with divine goodness and prophecy (e.g., 'knowledge shall be increased') to morally and rhetorically support scientific enterprise.
